transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-20 10:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE); Maya Chen (Redwood SE); Alex Ruiz (Redwood CSM); Dr. Priya Nair (Veridian ML Lead); Carlos Mendes (Veridian Infra); Linda Park (Veridian Product)

Summary: Weekly POC sync focused on throughput optimization. Reviewed last week's benchmark (continuous batching + concurrency adjustments), discussed queueing behavior under bursts, explored kernel-level GPU bottlenecks, and agreed on next steps (24h load run, send perf logs, update pricing/commit options). Some transcription errors and name mis-hearings present.

Topics: throughput, continuous batching, batch target sizing, concurrency targets, tail latency, queueing/backpressure, dedicated vs hosted routing, burst capacity, perf logs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: all right good morning everyone uh thanks for joining, this is our weekly poc sync on throughput optim. we did a quick update last week, this week we have the 10k-run results and kernel traces so maya will walk through those.
[00:18] Maya: hey hi, yeah i'll share screen i have the summary, cliff notes first - steady state we saw about 18% improvement in tokens/sec with continuous batching enabled, and p95 latency improved slightly for the short requests, but for the long prompt tail we still see spikes.
[00:36] Dr. Priya: okay that matches our observations, we saw sudden queue growth when we pushed concurrency above 60, it looked like requests were piling into the dispatcher, is that what you saw?
[00:49] Maya: yeah so couple of things - when concurrency hits the model worker pool limit the dispatcher starts to accumulate and batching windows stretch, plus kv-cache misses had a compounding effect. i have a kernel timeline that shows longer som-e kernel waits during mem copies.
[01:12] Carlos: can you explain kv cache misses? we thought the cache was enabled across requests.
[01:19] Maya: sorry, yeah, so we have prefix caching and kv cache; in this workload there are frequent prompt churns so many requests don't hit the cache and cause re-attenuation which increases per-token compute. that plus partial batches increases latency.
[01:37] Samir: two knobs we usually tune: target batch size and max concurrency. we also can enable aggressive prefix caching for sessions pinned to customers, but that requires sticky routing on customer side or session affinity.
[01:52] Linda: sticky routing would be fine for us as long as fallback exists for host failures. we can't have single-threaded hotspots.
[02:02] Maya: yes we recommend canary sticky + fallback to non-sticky if worker health drops. also we can set a queue depth limit to backpressure the client and keep latency SLOs.
[02:17] Dr. Priya: curious about the burst behavior - we had a sudden 5x spike; the tokens/sec dropped but cpu/gpu util looked under 80% while queueing grew. is that expected?
[02:31] Maya: that pattern usually means batching windows are too short or concurrency is too low, causing more small batches and overhead; or the kernel scheduling results in stalls - the GPU isn't the bottleneck, it's that the host-side batching pipeline can't keep steady large batches.
[02:50] Samir: right, so either increase concurrency (more inflight requests) to build larger batches, or increase the batching window (wait a few ms to coalesce). tradeoff is latency.
[03:03] Carlos: we care about 95th latency under 600ms for short calls, but also need throughput for nightly jobs. we can accept slightly higher p95 for long prompts.
[03:15] Maya: recommended setting from infra experiments: for your mix (70% short, 30% long), target batch size 24-32, concurrency target ~70-90 per model shard. that kept p95 ~450-500ms and improved tokens/sec.
[03:34] Dr. Priya: is that per-GPU or per-shard? our shard mapping is 2shards per GPU at 8k context.
[03:42] Maya: per model worker shard. so you need to multiply by shard count. if you have 2 shards per GPU, you'll end up looking at 140-180 inflight across the node.
[03:52] Alex: quick note - if you go that high we recommend monitoring page cache and memory pressure, we saw some OOM-ish pauses in the earlier run.
[04:02] Carlos: yes we observed occasional worker restarts around minute 18 in the last run, probably due to OOMs. logs attached in the s3 link.
[04:12] Maya: the kernel traces show a handful of outliers around memcpy peaks. my hypothesis is occasional GC-like activity in the runtime causing larger mem copy ops. we'll correlate with allocator logs.
[04:28] Dr. Priya: okay, so concrete config changes to try this week?
[04:34] Samir: Maya propose config A: increase max concurrency to 80, batch target 28, batching window 8ms, queue_depth_limit 200. Config B: keep concurrency 60, increase batching window to 15ms, batch target 32 - B favors throughput but could increase p95 for short calls.
[04:56] Maya: we ran both in lab for 10k requests - config A hit target p95 ~480ms and tokens/sec +12% vs baseline; config B gave +18% tokens/sec but p95 for short calls jumped to ~680ms in some bursts.
[05:14] Linda: leaning to A then, because product needs responsive UI.
[05:20] Samir: makes sense. we can also enable adaptive batching heuristics - start with A and allow short-window growth if queue builds for longer prompts.
[05:32] Carlos: what's the recommended concurrency cap to avoid worker oom? i.e. safe ceiling.
[05:38] Maya: based on your memory profile, i'd cap per-shard concurrency at 95 and node-wide at 180; also enable soft memory limits and eviction.
[05:52] Dr. Priya: you mentioned prefix caching earlier - how much win does that give?
[05:58] Maya: in our tests with high session affinity, prefix caching reduced per-token computation for repeated contexts by roughly 25-35% and reduced p95 tail significantly. but it requires session stickiness.
[06:12] Samir: and we can route by policy - dedicated pool for critical paths + hosted fallback. for this pilot we recommend dedicated pool with burst capacity to hosted for extreme spikes.
[06:24] Carlos: cost question - will burst to hosted materially increase unit cost?
[06:29] Samir: yes it'll be higher per-token during bursts but overall reduced infra cost vs overprovisioning for rare extreme peaks. we'll model it in the pricing send.
[06:40] Dr. Priya: any security concerns with routing to hosted for some data? we have PHI in certain prompts.
[06:47] Samir: yes that matters - if any PHI involved you shouldn't route to hosted. for that use-case we'd keep it on private/dedicated and consider pre-warming capacity or reserved capacity commits.
[06:58] Maya: alternatively, we could encrypt payloads with customer KMS and audit logs but some customers still want full on-prem for PHI.
[07:09] Linda: okay we'll mark sensitive workflows and keep them in-dedicated.
[07:15] Carlos: back to the perf run, maya you said kernel traces - can you summarize top 3 hotspots?
[07:22] Maya: sure: 1) memcpy peaks during kv-cache populates, 2) occasional cuda kernel launch latency variance on block reductions, 3) host-side batching queue locks when many small batches arrive.
[07:38] Dr. Priya: any quick mitigations for memcpy peaks?
[07:42] Maya: we can pre-alloc buffers, use pinned memory for host->device copies, and tune allocator GC thresholds. those reduced peaks in our experiments by ~40%.
[07:55] Samir: we'll include recommended allocator settings in the config doc.
[08:01] Alex: implemented notes: alex mentioned earlier that we should watch for node level sched spikes when concurrency increases - we'll add a dashboard panel for queue length and worker free slots.
[08:14] Carlos: on the load test you want us to run, please confirm exact traffic profile — mix of prompt lengths and QPS.
[08:20] Maya: we'll send the exact load profile. quick summary: 70% short (<256 tokens) at 80 rps baseline with bumps to 450 rps for 60s bursts; 30% long (1k-2k tokens) at 5 rps. run for 24h. set concurrency target=80 for config A.
[08:38] Dr. Priya: will do.
[08:41] Samir: also monitoring: please capture kernel traces every 5 minutes and upload so we can correlate spikes.
[08:48] Maya: we'll provide a small agent script to collect nsys-like traces and the perf csvs.
[08:53] Linda: about cost modeling - samir you mentioned reserved vs burst - can you give us a cost delta?
[08:59] Samir: rough numbers: reserved monthly for your projected baseline ~ $Xk/month; with burst to hosted we'd estimate +30-40% in peak month but lower steady infra. i'll put precise numbers in the email.
[09:12] Carlos: any gotchas re: model quantization? we plan to use q4 for cheaper cost.
[09:17] Maya: q4 gives reduced memory and improved throughput but slightly lower quality for some prompts. for retrieval use-cases it's usually fine; for clinical summarization we prefer q8 or 16-bit to preserve fidelity.
[09:29] Dr. Priya: okay we'll keep long form clinical summarization on higher precision.
[09:34] Samir: quick recap of decisions: go with config A for next run (concurrency 80, batch target 28, batching window 8ms, queue_depth_limit 200), enable aggregator pinned sessions for non-sensitive flows, and run 24h load test.
[09:51] Maya: i'll share perf logs and kernel traces and also a suggested conf file for the runtime.
[09:57] Linda: samir i'll need the pricing doc before friday so i can review with finance.
[10:02] Samir: yes i'll send by Friday EOD.
[10:06] Dr. Priya: one more question - how will Redwood handle graceful degradation if a worker node dies mid-batch? we saw partial failures before.
[10:14] Maya: runtime does partial batch rollback and re-dispatch but that adds latency; recommended is multi-shard replication or application-level retry with idempotency. we can enable fast-fail policy to reduce slow tails.
[10:27] Carlos: good, we'll check logs from the restart event.
[10:30] Alex: cool. any other risks?
[10:33] Linda: none from product side.
[10:35] Samir: ok next steps recap: samir send pricing + burst notes; maya send perf logs + suggested runtime config; carlos run 24h load; linda confirm success criteria; we meet 2026-05-28 for follow-up.
[10:49] Meeting end.

References/links mentioned: s3://veridian-poc/logs/2026-05-18, shared drive: /redwood/poc/veridian/perf-2026-05-18.csv, kernel traces s3 link (will be shared by Maya).

Notes on transcription: some names transcribed inconsistently (e.g., KV cache -> K V cache; references to "RedWood Dedicated" instead of Redwood Dedicated). Occasional filler words removed for readability but overall conversational transcript retained.
